A Controlled Study of Models, Skills,
Feedback, and Curriculum
in Agentic Robotics

Kaiyuan Chen    Xinyue Zhu    Shuangyu Xie Affiliation: UC Berkeley*Equal contribution    Uksang Yoo Affiliation: UC Berkeley*Equal contribution    Thi Thu Phuong Luong Affiliation: Bosch    Marcus Gualtieri Affiliation: Bosch    Christian Juette Affiliation: Bosch    Liu Ren Affiliation: Bosch    Spencer Huang Affiliation: NVIDIA    Ken Goldberg Affiliation: UC Berkeley*Equal contribution
Abstract

Agentic robotics asks coding agents to implement and iteratively improve robot policies from simulated and real-world physical interactions. We study the self-learning loop of agentic robotics through a controlled simulation study spanning nine manipulation tasks, 631 different experiment configurations, and 28K coding agent rollouts, systematically varying model capability, skill priors, feedback structure, and curriculum. The experiment data suggests that the bottleneck is often not the access to sufficient information, but interpreting it into the right policy update. Across these factors, a successful self-learning loop depends on how effectively agents attribute failures, reason task-relevant spatial and geometric structure, and selectively restructure code to improve policies.

1 Introduction

Recent coding agents, such as GPT Astra  (OpenAI, 2026a) and Claude Fable  (Anthropic, 2026a), have become increasingly capable of generating and iteratively repairing executable programs, motivating a growing class of Agentic Robotics (AR) systems in which LLM- and VLM-based agents write code that composes perception, planning, and control skills into robot policies (Liang et al., 2023b; Singh et al., 2023; Fu et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026a). However, self-improvement in robotics differs fundamentally from software debugging. In software, failures, such as compiler errors, are often exposed through symbolic feedback that is already closely aligned with the program; but in robotics, the evidence to improve a policy is instead embedded in physical interactions: object geometry, spatial relationships, contact, motion, and changes in the scene over time. As illustrated in Figure 1, a failed placement can be attributed to an earlier incompatible grasp and a collision requires reasoning about the geometry of an object after it becomes part of the moving robot. In this paper, we ask: what determines whether an agent can interpret physical interaction and convert it into effective robot-policy improvement?

We design a controlled simulation study of agentic robot self-learning across five contact-rich VABAR manipulation tasks Xie et al. (2026b) and four longer-horizon MimicGen tasks Mandlekar et al. (2023). Holding the overall self-learning harness fixed, we systematically vary four components of the learning loop: model capability, skill prior, feedback structure, and curriculum, as illustrated in Figure 2. Across these studies, we find that self-learning is limited less by the availability of useful information than by the agent’s ability to turn the information into effective policy updates. More execution feedback is not necessarily more useful: feedback is most effective when aligned with semantically meaningful policy decisions rather than reported at the finest temporal resolution. Similarly, world-frame states contain all the information needed for manipulation, yet agents often fail to recover task-relevant object-relative and functional relationships unless these are made explicit. Even when agents identify local geometric errors, they often struggle to translate them into coherent collision-aware motion plans. We find that this limitation can also affect curriculum design: agents tend to preserve and patch policy structure inherited from earlier stages rather than fundamentally reorganize it, so privileged learning can either provide a useful initialization or constrain later learning when the inherited policy depends on privileged precision or brittle manipulation strategies. Our results further suggest that progress in agentic robot self-learning comes from the better structures of skills, feedback, and state representations and the learned physical reasoning ability from the underlying models.

This paper makes three contributions: (1) A controlled study design for Agentic Robotics that isolates four important components of simulation-guided self-learning, (2) Experiment data from 631 implemented experiments with 28 thousand simulation rollouts on Agentic robotics policies, (3) Six findings on model capability, skill priors, feedback structure, and curriculum.

2 Related Work

Agentic Robotics. Foundation models have been used to compose robot skills and generate executable policies through language-model planning and code generation (Liang et al., 2023a; Ahn et al., 2023; Singh et al., 2023). More recent work integrates foundation models with explicit spatial representations, geometric constraints, and task-and-motion planning to support open-vocabulary and multi-step manipulation (Huang et al., 2023a; Huang et al., 2024b; Shen et al., 2026; Murray et al., 2025). Other approaches close the loop by using simulation or real-world execution feedback to revise policies, acquire skills, and improve task performance over repeated interactions (Fu et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026a; Xiao et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026). Rather than introducing a new agent architecture, we study how individual components of this self-learning loop affect performance.

Controlled Evaluation of Agentic Robotics. Robot-learning benchmarks increasingly use standardized task suites to evaluate generalization, long-horizon reasoning, and manipulation under controlled variation (Gu et al., 2023; Li et al., 2022; Mees et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2022). More recent benchmarks extend controlled evaluation to foundation-model agents by measuring interactive decision making, embodied reasoning, perception, and action across diverse environments (Liu et al., 2024; Manling Li et al., 2024; Rui Yang et al., 2025). Robot-specific evaluations further study robot-centric perception and decision making, coding-agent behavior under different abstraction and interaction settings, and repeated manipulation under controlled task variation (Xie et al., 2026a; Fu et al., 2026; Xie et al., 2026b). Unlike prior agentic robotics benchmarks that primarily vary tasks, environments, or complete agent systems, we hold the self-learning harness fixed and independently vary model capability, skill priors, feedback structure, and curriculum to isolate how each factor affects initial policy generation and subsequent self-improvement.

Skills, Feedback, and Curriculum for Self-Learning. Prior work has shown that reusable skills and execution feedback can improve embodied agent learning (Ahn et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2023b; Fu et al., 2026). Skill libraries provide reusable action abstractions that constrain generation and support compositional behavior, while systems such as Voyager jointly combine an executable skill library, environment feedback, and an automatic curriculum for continual improvement (Wang et al., 2024). More broadly, language agents can use environment observations, linguistic critiques, or tool-derived feedback to revise plans and outputs across interaction or repeated attempts (Yao et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023; Madaan et al., 2023; Gou et al., 2024). However, prior work also shows that self-correction can be unreliable without sufficiently informative external feedback (Huang et al., 2024a). Curriculum learning instead structures the progression of experience (Bengio et al., 2009), while privileged-information methods use state available during training to simplify learning before transferring to image-based or otherwise non-privileged observations (Pinto et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2020). These factors are often introduced jointly within a single system. We instead study them separately by varying the skill prior, temporal and spatial feedback representation, and privileged-to-vision curriculum.

3 Problem Formulation

Agentic robotics for manipulation.

A robot manipulation task class can be defined as a tuple 𝒯=⟨ℒ,ℰ,ℛ,𝒪,𝒳,ℬ,𝒥⟩\mathcal{T}=\langle\mathcal{L},\mathcal{E},\mathcal{R},\mathcal{O},\mathcal{X},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{J}\rangle: a natural-language instruction ℒ\mathcal{L}, a fixed workcell ℰ\mathcal{E} with a known robot and sensor configuration ℛ\mathcal{R}, a bounded set of objects 𝒪\mathcal{O} with known models, a state space 𝒳\mathcal{X} of robot configurations and object poses, a belief space ℬ\mathcal{B} giving the distribution over initial object poses, and a reward 𝒥\mathcal{J}, here the per-object success indicator 𝕀⁡(success)\mathbb{I}(\text{success}). A task instance τi=⟨oi,xi⟩\tau_{i}=\langle o_{i},x_{i}\rangle is drawn from 𝒪\mathcal{O} and ℬ\mathcal{B}. The agent produces a policy π\pi represented as executable source code composed from reusable robot skills. Following the graph-based policy representation of GaP (Chen et al., 2026a), we view π\pi as a computation graph whose nodes invoke skills and whose edges define their execution and control flow. The policy is constructed over a skill library 𝒮=𝒮0∪𝒮g∪𝒮τ∪𝒮A\mathcal{S}=\mathcal{S}_{0}\cup\mathcal{S}_{g}\cup\mathcal{S}_{\tau}\cup\mathcal{S}_{A}, where 𝒮0\mathcal{S}_{0} contains basic robot and sensor primitives; 𝒮g\mathcal{S}_{g} contains reusable general-purpose skills; 𝒮τ\mathcal{S}_{\tau} contains task-specific skills provided by a human expert; and 𝒮A\mathcal{S}_{A} contains task-specific skills synthesized by the agent. Given 𝒮\mathcal{S}, an LLM agent AA constructs π\pi by selecting, parameterizing, and composing available skills, while implementing new skills when the existing library is insufficient.

On a task instance τi\tau_{i}, the resulting policy π⁡(a∣ℐ)\pi(a\mid\mathcal{I}) maps observations ℐ\mathcal{I} to robot actions aa in closed loop, and the resulting episode is evaluated by 𝒥\mathcal{J}. Given a task class 𝒯\mathcal{T} and skill library 𝒮\mathcal{S}, the agent seeks to construct a policy that succeeds across the belief space: π∗=arg⁡maxπ​𝔼xi∼ℬ​[𝒥⁡(π⁡(a∣ℐ))],\pi^{*}=\arg\max_{\pi}\;\mathbb{E}_{x_{i}\sim\mathcal{B}}\left[\mathcal{J}\big(\pi(a\mid\mathcal{I})\big)\right], using only ℒ\mathcal{L}, 𝒮\mathcal{S}, and the outcomes of its own policies. Policy improvement may therefore modify both the composition of the policy graph and the implementation of its constituent skills.

Self-learning loop.

Unlike reinforcement learning, feedback in the self-learning loop is not restricted to a scalar reward. At iteration kk, the current policy πk\pi_{k} runs in simulation on the training instances {τi}\{\tau_{i}\}. A feedback function FF turns these runs into a textual (and optionally visual) report fk=F⁡(πk,{τi})f_{k}=F(\pi_{k},\{\tau_{i}\}). The agent then edits its own policy, conditioned on the report and on its edit history πk+1=A⁡(πk,fk,{(πj,fj)}j<k)\pi_{k+1}=A\big(\pi_{k},\,f_{k},\,\{(\pi_{j},f_{j})\}_{j<k}\big). The loop runs for KK iterations. Success is reported on a held-out set of instances for the initial policy π0\pi_{0} (zero-shot, k=0k{=}0) and for the iterate with the best validation score, πk∗\pi_{k^{*}} with k∗=arg⁡maxk⁡val⁡(πk)k^{*}=\arg\max_{k}\mathrm{val}(\pi_{k}). Held-out success at every iteration gives a learning curve for each setting and task. Each study below varies one component of this loop: the agent AA, the skills 𝒮\mathcal{S}, the feedback FF, or the curriculum over training instances.

Assumptions and Scope.

We assume access to a reliable physics simulator. Training and evaluation remain within the same manipulation task class, with a fixed robot and sensor configuration and bounded scene variation. We evaluate generalization to held-out instances of these task classes and do not study sim-to-real transfer or generalization to new embodiments.

4 Study Design

Task Setup.

We evaluate five simulated manipulation tasks from the Variational Automation Benchmark for Agentic Robotics (VABAR) Xie et al. (2026b): (1) Tool Hanging, (2) Syringe Packing, (3) Gear Meshing, (4) USB-C Insertion, and (5) Cable Routing. For the curriculum study, we evaluate four multi-step tasks from MimicGen Mandlekar et al. (2023) using the Medium (D1) layouts: (1) Kitchen, (2) Coffee, (3) Threading, and (4) Mug Cleanup (Figure 3).

Skill Setup.

We use open-robot-skills provided by  Chen et al. (2026a) as task-agnostic skill library 𝒮\mathcal{S}. The library contains a set of 30 skills in the Agent Skills format, each with a natural-language SKILL.md describing when the skill applies and conditions. The library covers perception, grasping and motion planning primitives. The full list of skills can be found in Appendix B.

Metrics and Evaluation scale. In evaluation, every agent setting runs the same closed-loop episodes on the same training, validation and testing task instances with repeated runs. We report the success rate of the hold-out testing task instance that the scene configuration is different from the training and testing task instances. We run each of the ten agent settings on the five tasks with five independent runs per task with two rounds of feedback. In each round the current program runs on 4 training, 5 validation and 10 held-out instances. We use full spatial and temporal feedback and no curriculum for the skill composition study and spatial temporal skill expansion study. We use Opus 5 xhigh as default for the feedback and skill-library studies. Including pilot studies, we use 17,900 GPU-hours on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs and 2,700 GPU-hours on NVIDIA A100 with in total 27,600 coding agent rollouts with an estimation of $70,000 computing cost. The study takes 2,500 coding agents editing sessions with $36,500 for LLM inference cost.

5 Experiments

5.1 Agent Model

We study how the choice of coding model affects both initial policy generation and subsequent self-learning. Each agent is given the shared general skill library, and the task-specific expert skills provided with VABAR( Xie et al. (2026b)). The skill library is sufficiently expressive for successful task execution. Each agent generates a zero-shot policy (@​0@0) and then revises its code from execution feedback for two rounds (@​1@1 and @​2@2). We evaluate Claude Opus 5 (Anthropic, 2026b), Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic, 2026c), Claude Sonnet 5 (Anthropic, 2026d), Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic, 2026a), GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI, 2026a), GPT-6 Sol (OpenAI, 2026b), DeepSeek V4 (DeepSeek-AI, 2026), and Kimi K3 (Kimi Team, 2026). Table 1 reports held-out success after each round, and Figure 5 analyzes how models construct their initial policies from provided and generated skills.

Table 1 shows zero-shot performance is not sufficient to evaluate if the model can self-improve. Several models begin from nearly identical initial success rates but diverge after receiving the same execution feedback. For example, Opus 5 xhigh, Fable 5.1, GPT-6 Astra, and Sonnet 5 start at 43–45% overall success, yet after two rounds Opus 5 xhigh and Fable 5.1 improve to 74% and 64%, respectively, while GPT-6 Astra and Sonnet 5 remain at 48% and 46%. The same distinction appears across individual tasks: models that initially fail Tool Hanging or USB-C Insertion can sometimes repair these policies substantially, whereas others remain near their initial performance despite observing the same failures. Opus 5.5 is strong at both stages, increasing from 67% zero-shot to 77% after feedback. These results suggest that generating a plausible initial manipulation policy and using execution evidence to diagnose and repair that policy are distinct model capabilities (Figure 4).

Finding 1. Differences in model capability are less apparent at policy initialization but become pronounced during self-learning. Models with similar zero-shot performance can diverge substantially after receiving the same execution feedback, suggesting that policy generation and policy repair are distinct capabilities.

5.2 Skill

We next study how agents use the skills they are given. The skill library provides an important prior: the expert skills encode task-specific manipulation strategies, while the general library provides reusable perception, grasping, and motion-planning routines. Such a library could help the agent by providing useful building blocks, or could instead constrain it to behaviors already represented in the library. To distinguish these cases, we trace the source of each line in the zero-shot policy (@​0@0). After normalizing each line, we match it verbatim against the expert task-specific skills, the general-library skills also used by the human policy, and the remaining general-library skills; unmatched lines are attributed to new code written by the agent.

Figure 5 reports the mean number of lines from each source, averaged over runs per task and then over tasks, and relates it to success after feedback in Table 1. As shown in Figure 5, models draw on the same skills in different ways. Models that improve most with feedback also write a larger share of their policy as new task-specific code: new code makes up 24% of the lines for Opus 5 xhigh, 18% for Opus 5.5, and 12% for Fable 5.1. They use the expert skills as a basis but add or modify task-specific logic where the provided implementations are insufficient. In contrast, Sonnet 5, DeepSeek V4, Kimi K3, and GPT-6 Astra write only 4–7% new code and rely more heavily on behavior already represented in the expert and general skills. These models also improve the least, ending at 39–46% overall success after two rounds. Using more of the library is not the same as adapting beyond it: Kimi K3 uses the largest share of general skills not used by the human policy (13% of its lines), yet still writes little new code and gains only 7 points. Since several of these models start from similar zero-shot success, the difference is not simply in the quality of the first policy, but in whether the agent can modify and extend the provided skills when the existing behavior is insufficient.

Finding 2. Expert skills are a boundary for weaker models but a scaffold for stronger ones. Weaker models largely compose behaviors already represented in the skill library, while stronger models selectively reuse and depart from human-provided skills to create new task-specific approaches.

5.3 Feedback

Temporal Failure Attribution. We next study whether self-learning agents can attribute an observed robot failure to the earlier policy decision that caused it. A manipulation episode consists of multiple perception, planning, and execution steps, so the point at which a failure becomes observable need not be the point at which the underlying error was introduced. As shown in Figure 6, the policy skill selected for repair can occur throughout the preceding trajectory, sometimes substantially before the point at which the episode finally halts. We therefore ask whether exposing intermediate execution outcomes helps the agent identify which earlier policy step should be revised.

Table 2 shows that the localized temporal feedback depends on where the underlying error occurs relative to where the failure becomes observable. Reporting every motion primitive can expose an earlier error once it manifests as incorrect motion, reaching 45% on Tool Hanging and 80% on Gear Meshing. However, this finer-grained feedback does not expose non-motion operations such as perception. The useful unit of feedback is therefore the intermediate outcome associated with a meaningful policy decision, rather than the finest available time step. In Tool Hanging, the per-episode agent repeatedly attributed failure to the final reaching stage and modified that part of the policy, reaching only 7% held-out success. The observed miss, however, originated from an earlier incorrect estimate of the wrench ring. Skill-level feedback records the state changes and return values around each semantic step, exposing this earlier error and increasing held-out success to 90%. Gear Meshing shows the same pattern, improving from 10% to 70%. Conversely, localized temporal feedback is less useful when the cause of failure is already apparent in the final state. In Syringe Packing, a syringe left outside or across the container opening directly exposes the relevant geometric failure, and per-episode feedback reaches 90% held-out success.

Finding 3. Feedback can be more useful when reported at the level of semantically meaningful policy skills, not simply at the finest temporal resolution. In multi-stage manipulation, the observed failure can occur well after the decision that caused it. Skill-level feedback exposes the intermediate outcomes of meaningful policy decisions and improves failure attribution, while finer motion-level feedback misses non-motion decisions such as perception.

Spatial and Geometric Representation

We next study whether the representation of execution state affects an agent’s ability to reason about spatial failures. A conventional world-frame representation describes where objects are, but leaves the agent to reconstruct the object-relative quantities needed for manipulation. As suggests in Table 3, the world-frame state is sufficient in principle to recover the manipulation-relevant quantities, the agent often fails to reliably compose the required coordinate transformations and connect them to a policy decision. Object-frame feedback makes these same relationships explicit, such as grasp offsets and relative orientations, and substantially improves performance on Tool Hanging and, to a lesser extent, Gear Meshing. This suggests that information completeness alone is insufficient, and agents can possess the necessary coordinates yet still fail to derive the spatial relationships needed for manipulation. The same limitation extends beyond coordinate frames to object geometry itself. Providing accurate object state and geometry does not mean the agent understands how that geometry constrains action, because inferring the affordance features of the wrench and hanger from whole-object poses is challenging for agents. Part annotations further improve feedback by exposing the functional structures that matter for interaction. Part-annotated feedback reaches 52% overall success, compared with 40% for object frames and 30% for world-frame state and relations.

Finding 4. Recovering task-relevant spatial and geometric relationships from raw state information remains a bottleneck for agentic robotics. Although world-frame and object-frame feedback describe the same underlying scene, agents perform substantially better when object-relative geometry and functional spatial relationships are explicitly available, rather than requiring them to derive them.

Feedback Reasoning.

We next study how self-learning agents translate spatial understanding into executable robot motion. We compare how human-written and agent-learnt policies structure perception, motion planning, and recovery. Figure 8 shows that human policies frequently make geometric structure explicit through repeated perception and re-registration, intermediate waypoints, and dedicated motion-planning stages. These intermediate poses encode geometric priors such as approaching from a safer direction, maintaining clearance, or moving through configurations from which a feasible motion is easier to find. In contrast, self-learning agents more often use verification, retry, and recovery around coarser manipulation steps. They can reuse motions containing useful geometric structure, but are less consistent at reconstructing why that structure is necessary when generating or modifying the policy themselves.

Syringe Packing provides a concrete example. The robot must carry a 150 mm syringe through a 55 mm opening while reasoning about the syringe as part of the moving system, surrounding obstacles, reorientation clearance, and insertion orientation (Figure 11). The human policy represents these dependencies explicitly with a collision world, held-object registration, collision-aware waypoints, and orientation-constrained insertion.

In contrast, none of the agent runs without expert skills independently constructed an equivalent collision representation, and 17 of 19 initial self-written policies carried or released the syringe flat over the opening. Feedback often allowed agents to recognize the resulting errors and eventually adopt heuristics such as reorienting above the lid and descending vertically, but they still tended to encode these fixes as clearance constants, staging heights, and retries rather than as a general collision-aware model.

Finding 5. Reasoning over collision geometry and spatial relationships remains a key bottleneck for agentic robot motion planning. Agents can recognize local geometric errors, but struggle to integrate object pose, held-object geometry, obstacles, and clearance into a coherent collision-aware motion plan.

5.4 Curriculum Design

We study a representative privileged-to-perception curriculum, a common design in reinforcement learning and used in prior works such as Pinto et al. (2017); Chen et al. (2020). As a focused case study of curriculum transfer in agentic robotics, the agent first learns with privileged simulation states with exact simulator geometry and is then transferred to non-privileged simulation states such as RGB-D perception. We evaluate this curriculum on four MimicGen tasks using their Medium (D1) layouts with 8 privileged and 8 perception iterations and Claude Fable 5.1. We also use three VABAR tasks: Tool Hanging (Level 2), Gear Meshing (Level 2), and USB-C Insertion (Level 1) with 5 privileged iterations and 5 perception iterations with Claude Opus 5. Figure 10 reports results on four MimicGen and three VABAR tasks. Exact task configurations, training and held-out layouts, iteration budgets, probe settings, and other protocol details are provided in Appendix J.

Figure 10 suggests that privileged-to-perception learning does not uniformly improve over learning directly from perception. Privileged information removes perception uncertainty during early learning, but, as suggested by Findings 4 and 5, accurate geometry alone does not guarantee that the agent discovers the right spatial representation or manipulation strategy. The privileged phase can learn useful task structure, as in Threading, Coffee, and Mug Cleanup, but it can also sometimes commit early to brittle or non-generalizable choices. For example, Kitchen develops a grasp strategy that depends on geometric precision unavailable after transfer, while Tool Hanging remains below 10% held-out success during privileged learning despite access to exact wrench geometry. Thus, privileged information can simplify the learning problem without necessarily producing a policy that remains appropriate under perception. We further visualize and analyze representative failure cases in Appendix J.2.

In addition, Table 4 further suggests that once a policy structure is established under privileged state, subsequent perception-based learning tends to preserve and patch that structure rather than fundamentally reorganize it (which corresponds to Finding 1). Across tasks, the privileged-to-perception policies change little in size after transfer, from 12.0 skills at the end of the privileged phase to 12.7 after perception learning on average, while the final perception-only policies contain 16.1 skills. The resulting path dependence can be beneficial when the early structure captures a manipulation strategy that remains valid under vision, but this can be harmful when the structure assumes geometric precision unavailable from perception. In such cases, the curriculum does not merely provide an initialization; it can constrain subsequent self-learning.

Finding 6. Privileged-to-perception curriculum learning can either accelerate or constrain subsequent perception-based learning. Privileged agents learn policies that rely on exact state, usually with less verification and recovery, and often retain this structure after transfer. This helps when the learned manipulation strategy remains valid, allowing perception learning to focus on perception errors, but hurts when the policy depends on state precision unavailable under perception or lacks mechanisms for handling perceptual uncertainty.

6 Discussion and Limitations

Our results return to the central question of this study: what determines whether an agent can interpret physical interaction and convert it into effective robot-policy improvement? Figure 11 provides a complementary view across the experiments. Only 7.3% of the human-solvable Level-1 test cases are solved by zero-shot policy generation alone, but the results suggest that improving agentic robotics requires the combination of iterative self-learning with richer simulation feedback, human task skills, and more powerful models. At the same time, this decomposition shows that 4.1% of test cases solved by a human-written policy under the same robot and simulation setup remain unsolved by the agents. Moreover, this study primarily considers Level-1 VABAR tasks with uncluttered environments and relatively simple motions. The remaining gap is concentrated in agents’ ability to interpret physical interaction into task-relevant reasoning and policy changes, particularly for spatial reasoning, manipulation planning, and collision-aware motion planning.

Limitations. This study does not cover the full range of conditions that may affect agentic robot self-learning, such as prompting strategies and harness configurations. Given the large number of agent rollouts required for controlled evaluation, we leave a broader study of these factors to future work. Our model comparison is also necessarily a snapshot in time, as new agent models are released frequently; we plan to update the evaluation as new models become available. We focus on simulation to enable repeatable evaluation, leaving sim-to-real transfer and adaptation to real-world feedback as important next steps; real-to-sim toolkits such as RoboSimStudio (Chen et al., 2026b) may make it easier to construct matching simulations of real tasks for such studies. Finally, we do not consider human-in-the-loop self-learning, where human feedback may complement autonomous simulation feedback during policy improvement.

Appendix

The appendix documents what is needed to read, check and reproduce the study, in three parts. Experimental setup (Appendices A–H) specifies the tasks, how they are scored and how their instances are drawn; the skill library and what each experiment ships; the self-learning harness, its complete prompts and feedback reports, and its revert, stopping and selection rules; and the models, their inference settings and the compute and cost of the study. Additional results (Appendix I) locates where the programs fail. Curriculum study (Appendix J) details the privileged-to-perception experiments of Section 5.4.

Experimental Setup

 

Appendix A Tasks, Scoring and Instances

This appendix specifies the five VABAR tasks (Figure 3) at the level needed to reproduce a score: what each task demands (Appendix A.1), how an episode becomes per-object success, the metric of every table (Appendix A.2), and how the 4 training, 5 validation and 10 held-out instances of each task are drawn (Appendix A.3). Appendix A.4 then relates held-out success on each instance to the quantities it was drawn with.

A.1 Task Specifications

The five tasks are the Easy (Level-1) tier of VABAR Xie et al. (2026b). Every task instance is one RoboSimStudio task document that, with its suite, fixes the robot, the objects, the start layout, a step cap, a goal predicate and a reward (stated, or the share of goal clauses met). Table 5 summarizes the five tasks.

What each task demands.

Each task stresses a different part of a policy. Tool Hanging moves only the wrench, so its difficulty lies in a grasp that keeps the ring free and a collision-free carry onto the hook. Syringe Packing must turn each 150 mm syringe upright to pass the 55 mm aperture, twice, among obstacles; it is the longest task (a median episode of 11,345 control steps, and 22% of episodes reach the step cap against 2–5% elsewhere) and the collision-geometry example of Finding 5. Gear Meshing is the only task with a temporal goal: the gear must turn with the pinion for 1 s of simulated time after the button press, unheld. USB-C Insertion is the precision task, with 0.15 mm of clearance per side and a cable dragging on the plug. Cable Routing manipulates a deformable object directly, with three separately scored sub-goals.

Instruction, embodiment and perception.

The agent receives the document’s instruction verbatim; it is identical across a task’s 19 documents, so instances differ only in the drawn scene. Only Cable Routing is prompted as bimanual (Table 13). The motion stack and segmentation backend are fixed per task and identical in every run, so no comparison in the main text mixes back ends.

A.2 Goal Predicates and Scoring

An episode ends when the policy returns (after a 60-control-step settle, 120 for Gear Meshing), reaches the step cap or diverges, and a Syringe Packing or Gear Meshing episode also as soon as its goal holds. The simulator then reads the document’s goal, a predicate over object features, contacts and speeds; once and hold-for clauses track the whole episode. Listing A.2 gives the goal clauses.

Per-object success.

Success is scored per object with VABAR’s scorer: derive_trial_keys strips the modal wrappers and makes one trial per single-object goal, or one per (object, region) pair when a goal has several containment clauses (Table 5); release clauses belong to no trial, and a diverged episode fails every trial. Scoring objects rather than episodes keeps the partial progress of the two multi-object tasks: at the kept iterate, 43% of held-out Syringe Packing episodes place exactly one of the two syringes, and no Cable Routing program meets every trial on all ten layouts. Some readings were scored before this rule was final; they count one Syringe Packing trial per episode (part of the reference runs of the feedback and skill-library studies) or a seated gear as a met Gear Meshing goal (some Gear Meshing reference runs). The instance analysis (Appendix A.4) and the failure analysis (Appendix I) rescore every batch they use with the final rule.

Partial credit.

Each document also defines a partial-credit reward in [0,1][0,1] (Table 5), which the loop logs but no reported number uses, because it adds little to per-object success: over every training and held-out episode of the tables’ finished runs, 80% of Tool Hanging episodes sit exactly at the 1/31/3 floor, 3% of USB-C Insertion rewards lie strictly between 0 and 1, Gear Meshing’s is binary and Syringe Packing’s equals the share of syringes placed; only Cable Routing’s quarters add resolution.

A.3 Scene Generation and Splits

A Tool Hanging, USB-C Insertion or Cable Routing instance is its base document drawn once by the base’s sampler at a fixed seed, from NumPy’s default_rng(seed + episode) at episode 0. A Gear Meshing or Syringe Packing instance records its draw as start poses: each gear board is drawn at its own seed, its tooth count from one balanced draw over the 40 boards, and the 30 syringe layouts are drawn from one default_rng(0) stream (tray shifts at least 10 mm apart). Either way a document reproduces its scene exactly, so every setting runs the same episodes. Table 6 lists the samplers, the ranges of every randomized quantity, and the documents of each split; Figure 12 shows each instance’s draw. The agent reads feedback from the training episodes only; validation decides when a run stops and which iterate is kept; held-out success is only reported (Appendix C.1): Table 1’s @kk is the best held-out reading within kk rounds, and the other tables read the zero-shot program and the kept iterate.

Coverage gaps.

The splits are fixed document ids, not stratified, and nine training and validation draws leave parts of each sampling range to the held-out split alone. No Gear Meshing training board has 24 teeth and no validation board has 16. Training wrenches are offset at most +2.9 mm in xx (validation +7.4 mm), while 7 of the 10 held-out wrenches are offset 8–18 mm. Training and validation trays are shifted at most 27.6 mm toward −y-y, while 4 held-out trays are shifted 39–60 mm. Training and validation plugs are offset at most 7.2 mm toward −x-x, while 2 held-out plugs are offset 10.8–11.0 mm. Training cables bow by a fraction of at most +0.03 and validation cables by at most +0.20, while 6 held-out cables bow +0.15 to +0.68.

A.4 Held-Out Instance Difficulty

To see whether some held-out instances are systematically harder, we pool the runs of all three studies’ tables and compute, per held-out object, the share of programs that succeed on it, at k=0k{=}0 (each distinct zero-shot program once; seeded feedback arms share their reference’s) and at the kept iterate, scoring every program with the final per-object rule (Figure 13).

Success is mostly a property of the program.

On Gear Meshing and USB-C Insertion a program usually solves every held-out instance or none: 68% of zero-shot Gear Meshing programs solve all ten boards, and even at the kept iterate 84% of USB-C programs are all-or-nothing, with per-layout shares of 34–42% and no trend in the plug’s offset, including the two plugs beyond every training draw. Zero-shot Tool Hanging succeeds on 7–11% of programs on every layout. On these tasks a held-out score mostly counts the programs that work.

Layout effects present from the start.

Where success does vary across layouts, the variation coincides with coverage gaps. On the four Syringe Packing layouts whose tray lies beyond every training and validation tray in −y-y (two of them also in −x-x), the first syringe is placed by 26% of zero-shot and 40% of kept programs, against 58% on the other six, and grasp misses (G in Table 23) make up 21% of its kept-iterate failures there against 6% elsewhere; the second syringe is harder on every layout (23% against 51% at the kept iterate). On Cable Routing the peg seats stay at 56–93% at the kept iterate, but the port trial varies with the cable’s bow (12–68%): on the six layouts bowing +0.15 or more, 28% of zero-shot and 24% of kept programs reach the port, against 58% and 55% on the other four. These six layouts also have the most negative port yaws, which ten layouts cannot separate from the bow.

Gaps that open with learning.

On Gear Meshing and Tool Hanging the instances start out equal and learning separates them. Zero-shot Gear Meshing success is flat across tooth counts (70–72%), but the kept iterate fixes 26% of the zero-shot failures on 16-tooth boards against 46–52% on the others, leaving them at 69% against 78–79%: the 24-tooth boards, which no training board has, gain the most, and the 16-tooth boards, which no validation board has, the least. At the kept iterate the seven Tool Hanging wrenches offset +8 mm or more succeed for 28% of programs against 34% for the other three, with reach failures (T) twice as common on them (22% against 11% of failures), though single layouts of the two groups overlap (21–33% against 33–38%).

Implications.

Because every setting meets the same instances, the comparisons of Tables 1, 2 and 3 stay paired, but every task’s absolute held-out level includes instances beyond the training draws. These cost success from the start only on Syringe Packing and Cable Routing, and learning does not close those gaps: it narrows Syringe Packing’s from 31 to 18 points and leaves Cable Routing’s unchanged. Of the two gaps that open with learning, the larger (Gear Meshing, 10 points) lies where validation, which selects the kept iterate, has no instance, not where training has none.

Appendix B Skill Library

The agent composes its policy over 𝒮=𝒮0∪𝒮​g∪𝒮​τ∪𝒮A\mathcal{S}=\mathcal{S}_{0}\cup\mathcal{S}g\cup\mathcal{S}\tau\cup\mathcal{S}_{A} (Section 3), where 𝒮A\mathcal{S}_{A} is the code it writes. We first describe how a program uses a skill, the three parts the harness provides, and what each experiment ships; the skill-library study qualifies Finding 2.

B.1 Library Format and Use

The general skills and the tool bundles ship in the Agent Skills format: a directory with a SKILL.md (when the skill applies, its state flow, declared tools, required inputs and named exits) and scripts. Each subgraph of a program carries a skill label, the 𝒮g\mathcal{S}_{g} skill it runs or generated for a stage the agent wrote. With the source, the agent copies the skill’s scripts into its workflow; in the docs-callable arm a node names a script and the runtime resolves it from the named skill. Every run enforces its arm: the runtime loads only the shipped skills, the guard refuses other labels, and the library checkout is closed to the agent. All runs read open-robot-skills ed6ab27, except three early Table 1 runs, which read 113261b (the same skills, three scripts differ); the earliest reference runs read a 113261b working tree whose skills equal ed6ab27’s.

B.2 Primitive Tools (𝒮0\mathcal{S}_{0})

𝒮0\mathcal{S}_{0} holds 70 to 78 tools per task: robot primitives, the motion backend’s planner, six tool bundles (cuRobo planning, curve fitting, point-cloud geometry, Grounding DINO detection, SAM3 segmentation and tracking, a VLM) and, on USB-C Insertion and Cable Routing, a few audited tools of the task’s own (Table 7). The agent gets SKILLS.md, which documents every tool, and the six bundle manuals; sim.check_success and the privileged sim.* state readers are withheld from every run, since the goal is what the agent has to learn. 𝒮0\mathcal{S}_{0} is thus not a set of bare primitives: detection, segmentation and grasp proposals are single calls.

B.3 General Skills (𝒮g\mathcal{S}_{g})

open-robot-skills holds 30 skills with 72 scripts (Table 8), most of them for perception (11) and grasping (8); five skills compute, plan and execute the motion of a held object. A run admits only skills whose scripts call nothing outside its 𝒮0\mathcal{S}_{0}, so no program reaches simulator state through a skill: three skills call withheld simulator tools and never ship, and the two executing-* skills need cuRobo’s motion.plan_to_pose. This leaves 27 callable skills on the cuRobo tasks and 25 on the OSC tasks.

B.4 Expert Skills (𝒮τ\mathcal{S}_{\tau})

For each task, 𝒮τ\mathcal{S}_{\tau} holds the scripts of the human-written VABAR vision policy (Table 9): 11 bundles with 43 entry scripts, the script nodes of each human graph without its wiring. Expert scripts carry no exit contract, so the agent copies what it uses into its own scripts and labels those subgraphs generated. 𝒮τ\mathcal{S}_{\tau} ranges from 17 entry scripts on Syringe Packing to a single glue script on Tool Hanging, whose human policy is built from 15 scripts of 10 skills in 𝒮g\mathcal{S}_{g}.

B.5 Availability per Experiment

Table 10 lists what each experiment ships and how many runs it has; every setting of Table 1 gets the whole library. The feedback study’s reference omits 𝒮τ\mathcal{S}_{\tau} because early zero-shot programs copied the human scripts, and a reference built on human code would measure that code more than the feedback. The skill-library study removes one part of the reference at a time: docs callable withholds the source but keeps every skill documented and callable, separating a skill’s interface from its code, and tools only removes 𝒮g\mathcal{S}_{g}.

Appendix C Agent Harness

Every run of Table 1 of the feedback study (Tables 2 and 3) executes the loop of Section 3 in one harness; the runs differ only in the agent and its reasoning budget, the shipped skills, the feedback renderer, the evaluation schedule and the time budgets. Each instance set has one role: the agent sees only the training episodes, validation decides when a run stops and which iterate it keeps, and the held-out set only measures. We follow one iteration of the loop (Appendix C.1), then give each study’s evaluation schedule (Appendix C.2) and the workspace and the checks a proposal passes (Appendix C.3). Appendices D and E reproduce what the agent reads, and Appendix F gives the revert, stopping and selection rules and relates the @kk of Table 1 to the validation-selected iterate.

C.1 Self-Learning Loop

At k=0k{=}0 the agent writes π0\pi_{0} from the task brief; every iteration then runs one unscored preflight episode on the first training instance, the four training episodes and, when scheduled, the held-out batch, and builds the feedback report from the training episodes alone, after the revert rule has chosen the policy the next session edits (Figure 14). The five validation episodes run after the report is written, for the stopping and selection rules (Appendix F); unless the run stops, a new agent session edits the policy into πk+1\pi_{k+1}. The session keeps no conversation from earlier sessions, but its report summarizes every earlier iterate (training result, edit, behavior and the previous session’s own account, Appendix E) and history/ holds the exact diffs. A rate limit that outlasts the retries of Table 18 defers the round without recording an iteration; any other provider error ends the session without an edit and counts as an unchanged iteration (1% of iterations).

C.2 Evaluation Schedule

Table 11 gives the schedule of each study and Appendix A the instance splits. Table 1 reports a learning curve, so it scores the held-out set every round; the 6-iteration studies report only π0\pi_{0} and the kept iterate, and score only those two.

Two first-pass runs of the Opus 5, xhigh row of Table 1 (Tool Hanging and Gear Meshing) depart from the splits: they train on the first training instance repeated four times and have no validation set (Appendix F.4). That row reuses the first three iterates of 6-iteration runs with the general and expert skills (𝒮g∪𝒮τ\mathcal{S}_{g}\cup\mathcal{S}_{\tau}); its @kk averages the runs with a held-out reading at round kk: the k=0k{=}0 reading, the kept iterate’s, one carried from an earlier stop, or a re-score of the k=1k{=}1 or k=2k{=}2 iterate on the same ten held-out instances after the run.

C.3 Workspace, Guard and Preflight

Workspace and sandbox.

Each session runs in a sealed workspace whose files Listing D.2 lists; workflow/ holds the policy and is the only directory the harness takes back. Claude Code runs with a deny list that blocks reading, listing and searching the simulator, the harness, the skill sources and all run outputs (the whole home directory), and with shell access limited to ./validate.sh (plus echo and mkdir). The Codex CLI cannot start its own sandbox on our machines, so its AGENTS.md states the same rules and off-limits paths, and the harness audits every command and file change of each session for those paths afterwards; no command or file change named one.

Guard.

A static guard accepts an improve session’s proposal only if every tool it names (tool nodes, recovery steps, literal ctx.tool("...") calls) is on the tier’s allowlist, no edited script computes a tool name at run time, every subgraph label names a shipped skill or marks the subgraph as the agent’s own, and ./validate.sh passes. π0\pi_{0} and preflight repairs skip the guard and are checked only by the ./validate.sh their session is asked to run. A rejected proposal returns to the agent with the violations for up to two fix rounds; one still rejected, or unchanged, carries the edited policy (πk\pi_{k}, or the incumbent after a revert) forward. The guard rejects 9% of first proposals, never for a withheld tool or an unshipped skill: every rejection is for a tool name computed at run time, which no static check can clear, and every rejected proposal passes after one fix round.

Preflight.

The preflight separates a policy that cannot run from one that runs and fails. Before anything is scored, an episode goes back to a fix session (up to two) if its graph fails to load or an error message carries a Python error no correct program raises (AttributeError, ImportError, IndexError, KeyError, NameError, SyntaxError, TypeError, UnboundLocalError, ZeroDivisionError), a tool-argument error or tool refusal, or one of a list of interpreter, tool-refusal and executor-binding messages. Any other error, such as a RuntimeError a policy raises to report a failure, counts as a failed episode. Capped at 1,500 steps, the preflight costs a broken program one short episode instead of a scored batch of identical failures. 3% of preflights crash (5% in the 3-iteration runs, 2% in the 6-iteration runs), mostly on TypeError, graphs that fail to load and tool-argument errors; fix sessions repair 88% of them, and the rest, all in 3-iteration runs, run their batch unrepaired. Table 12 counts these interventions per 100 agent sessions; preflights crash most often in the restricted skill-library arms (7.4 per 100 sessions), whose programs call raw tools or skills with hidden source.

Appendix D Prompts

Every coding-agent session starts in a sealed workspace, and the whole prompt is its instruction file INSTRUCTIONS.md: the session’s command-line prompt (Table 18) only points to that file, and we add no system prompt. INSTRUCTIONS.md is a task template with its {{slots}} filled, followed by a workspace block. We give the session templates, the workspace block, the slots whose values depend on the task, and what differs between the arms of a study. The templates are byte-identical in every harness snapshot the runs used.

D.1 Session Templates

A generate session (k=0k{=}0) reads Listing D.1; every improve session reads Listing D.1, with the feedback report in FEEDBACK.md (Appendix E). When the guard or the validator rejects a proposal, the next round edits the rejected proposal with Listing D.1 appended. When the unscored preflight episode raises a program error, a fix session runs the improve template with Listing D.1 appended.

The templates hold only task-independent advice. The generate brief asks for stages with a routable failure exit each, so that a failure ends the episode at a named step the report can name instead of exhausting the step budget. The improve brief names every channel a report may carry, including the stills that only the stills arm renders (Table 14), so that it is the same text under every feedback condition.

# Improve a robot policy from execution feedback

The task:

> {{instruction}}

The current workflow just ran in the simulator; its results are in the

feedback (per-episode outcomes and, depending on this experiment’s selected

channels, visual observations, structured state, state deltas, motion spans,

evaluator facts, or execution traces). Improve the policy so more episodes

succeed.

Run conditions: perception body **{{perception}}**, privilege tier

**{{privileged}}**, update mode **freeform** — you may change `workflow.json`

and any script, add scripts, or restructure the graph. Every tool you call

must be in `SKILLS.md`’s tier table, with a **literal** name string.

{{bimanual_note}}

How to use the feedback:

- If FEEDBACK.md opens with a **LOOP NOTICE**, the harness has already reset

`workflow/` to an earlier, better-scoring iteration: the feedback describes

the policy that regressed, not the one you are editing. Read it for what

the undone edits (in `history/kNNN.reverted.diff`) broke, then improve the

restored policy; do not re-apply the undone edits as they were.

- If the feedback lists captured frames, **Read the middle frame of the first

failed episode before diagnosing** — one image often shows what no number in

the packet can (an object resting on a lid, a hand pressed into a fixture).

- Diagnose before editing: find *where* each failed episode diverged (a wrong

grasp height reads differently from a drop mid-transport or a never-found

object).

- Prefer the smallest change that addresses the diagnosed failure; wholesale

rewrites discard what already works.

{{layout_note}}

- If every episode fails the same way at the same node, that node is the

problem; if failures are mixed, look for a fragile assumption upstream.

{{extra_guidance}}    

Listing 4: fix_validation.md, appended after a rejected proposal.      # Your previous proposal was rejected The guards/validator refused the last update for these reasons: ``` {{guard_feedback}} ``` Produce a corrected update that resolves every violation while keeping the intended improvement. Do not work around a violation by renaming or aliasing — fix the underlying edit.    

Listing 5: fix_preflight.md, appended after a preflight crash.      # Your policy could not run One episode was run before scoring this iteration, and the policy raised before it could finish: ``` {{preflight_feedback}} ``` These are program errors — a field read off a return value that does not carry it, a tool argument the tool does not declare, a name that was never bound. They are not failed grasps, so no episodes have been scored yet and none will be until the policy runs. Read the exact signatures in `SKILLS.md` before editing: the parameter names, and the keys each tool actually returns, are listed there. Fix the calls themselves rather than wrapping them in `try`/`except` — a swallowed error becomes a silent wrong answer, which costs a whole iteration to find.    

D.2 Workspace Instructions

Listing D.2 is appended to every brief. It names the workspace files and the one shell command the agent needs, and asks for a closing summary that the loop records as the iteration’s rationale; the next report quotes it as unverified (Listing E.3), next to the harness’s own account of the edit. In the workspace of a Fable 5.1 Tool Hanging run of Table 1, the files the block names take 126 KB: the workflow-format primer WORKFLOW_FORMAT.md (6.7 KB), the tool contract SKILLS.md (31 KB), the skill catalog SKILL_LIBRARY.md (21 KB), six tool-bundle manuals (30 KB) and the validator’s surface skills.lock.json (37 KB), next to the 28 shipped skill bundles. Codex sessions also find AGENTS.md (Listing D.2), which states the rules Claude Code enforces with its deny list (Appendix C.3).

D.3 Task-Specific Slots

Table 13 lists every slot and its value. Across tasks, only the instruction, the shipped skills, the Cable Routing bimanual note and the USB-C Insertion and Cable Routing guidance (Listings D.3 and D.3) differ. The layout note is in every brief because the reports print the training layouts’ world coordinates, which fit no held-out layout if copied into a policy. The bimanual note is set only for Cable Routing, whose expert policy anchors the cable’s far end with the support arm, while every motion verb drives arm 0 unless told otherwise.

The extra guidance states two facts no report shows. On these two tasks sam3.segment_text runs a color matcher that sam3.md does not describe, and its error for other queries blames missing SAM3 weights, which no edit can fix. And reports describe the scene but never the goal clause: in an early USB-C Insertion run, a report showed the plug 12.8 mm past the bore’s mouth, 0.2 mm off its axis and “seated in port.bore: yes” in an episode that scored zero, because the fingers still held it; once the brief stated the goal clause, the next training batch succeeded in all four episodes.

D.4 Differences Between Study Arms

Within a task, every feedback condition receives the same improve brief, byte for byte up to the earlier wording below, so the report is the only input that differs between the rows of Tables 2 and 3. Between the skill-library arms, the brief differs in the shipped-skill lines of the workspace block and in the Skills section of the workflow primer (Listings D.4–D.4); the skills themselves are in Appendix B.

First harness snapshot.

Runs launched on the first harness snapshot read an earlier wording of two passages; these are most runs of the reference configuration (the feedback reference and the full-library arm) and the Opus 5, xhigh runs of Table 1 that train on one layout. Their workspace block lacks the sentence “Run it exactly as written, from this directory—an absolute path to the same script is a different command and is refused, which costs a turn.”, and their primer ends the second paragraph of Listing D.4 with “… and copy its canonical_scripts into your scripts/ directory.” The rest of both texts is identical.

It is the right answer when nothing in the library fits, and the wrong one by default. `SKILL_LIBRARY.md` lists the strategies available in THIS run — already filtered to the tools you may call, so everything listed is runnable. Name one (`"skill": "proposing-short-axis-grasps"`), read that bundle’s `SKILL.md` under `skills/<name>/` for its state flow and hard rules, and reproduce its `canonical_scripts` into your `scripts/` directory with Read and Write — there is no shell copy here, and a `cp` costs you a refused turn. The reason this matters more than convenience: a stage usually has **more than one strategy**, and the library’s skills say so. A propose skill that declines ("the short axis is wider than this hand opens") hands you a routable exit to a *different* rung. A subgraph you wrote yourself has no such exit — when its one approach does not fit the object, the only move left is to re-tune numbers that cannot help, and the iteration is spent.

Appendix E Feedback Reports

One renderer turns the recorded training batch into FEEDBACK.md, the report fkf_{k} of Section 3 and the only feedback an improve session reads. We define the feedback conditions as settings of that renderer, list what each renders, walk through one report, compare one batch under every condition, and measure report length. The reference condition is the feedback of Table 1 and of the Per skill and + part annotations rows of Tables 2 and 3, which are the same runs.

E.1 Conditions

Each condition sets three axes of the renderer: the form of the report, its spatial representation and its temporal unit (Table 14). Every non-reference condition changes one axis of the reference, starts from the reference run’s initial policy, and first re-renders the reference’s own k=0k{=}0 training batch, so that differences between rows reflect the report rather than the initial policy.

E.2 What Each Condition Renders

Every condition renders the outcome block: per-episode and per-object success, steps, how each episode ended, and the errors the policy raised. Table 15 lists what each condition adds. Three consequences matter for reading the main tables. Outcome only is not a scalar reward: it names the node where each aborted episode raised and quotes the error, but not why a finished episode missed. A per-motion report has no unit for a step that moves nothing, so what a perception step returns never appears, the gap Finding 3 attributes to motion-level feedback. Syringe Packing declares no parts, so there the reference and object-frame reports differ only in wording, and the two rows end at the same 50% in Table 3. On Cable Routing the contact record omits the deformable cable, so no condition reports contact with the cable or a grasp or carry of it, and no close is reported as meeting the cable.

E.3 Report Anatomy

Listing E.3 is the opening of the reference report for the four training episodes that the first Tool Hanging reference run scored at k=0k{=}0: the task line, the legend naming the condition, the training result, the space conventions and declared parts, the episode table and the banners. One representative episode follows per failure signature (the first failing node, how the episode ended, the goals met), at most six, each followed by the other episodes that failed the same way, so a batch that fails one way costs one episode’s text.

From k=1k{=}1 the report summarizes every earlier iterate: its training result, its edit, what its policy did, derived from its own recorded run, and the previous session’s own account of its change, marked as unverified. When the training batch regresses under the revert rule (Appendix F.1), the loop restores the earlier iterate’s policy and the report opens with a notice, because the policy the agent now edits is no longer the one the report describes (Listing E.3).
