Reading the listings side by side.

Every report with relations says that the wrench never moved with the hand after the close; the state-only report gives the numbers without that verdict. The world-frame report gives the jaws’ offset from the wrench’s center as a world vector (0.123 m), which is an offset along the handle only because this wrench lies along world xx, a fact that report never states; object frames give the offset directly (+122 mm along the long axis), and part annotations add that the jaws closed 48 mm from the ring, the part the goal is written in. At the end of Episode 0, likewise, only part annotations relate the ring to the shank. The world-frame report holds the information but leaves the transform to the agent, the step Finding 4 finds unreliable. The per-episode report has no unit for the close, so a failure caused there is attributed to what the end state shows, and the per-motion report files the close under Motion 4, robot.close_gripper, which the agent must map back to its own graph step (Finding 3).

E.5 Report Size and Truncation

A report shows at most 12 outputs per node, each value cut to 60 characters, and at most 40 units per episode (the first and last four and those around the failing unit). Node errors are cut to 300 characters, a graph traceback to its last 1,500 characters, and the previous session’s account to 800 characters. The unit cap almost never binds (fewer than 1% of the reports behind Figure 15, all of them per-motion reports). Figure 15 shows how long the reports are: outcome-only reports stay near 3k characters, while state numbers and part geometry bring the reference to 21k, and Syringe Packing reports of Table 1 run to a median of 70k.

More text is not better.

Length does not predict learning. World-frame and object-frame reports have the same median length (16.9k characters), yet reach 30% and 40% overall held-out success (25% and 63% on Tool Hanging). The state-only report is nearly as long as the reference (18.2k against 20.8k) yet ends below outcome only at 3.0k, 11% against 19% overall. The per-motion report is a third shorter than the reference yet reaches 90% against 45% on Tool Hanging. Across the eight conditions, the rank correlation between median length and overall held-out success is 0.24: what helps is which quantities a report makes explicit and at which unit (Findings 3 and 4), not how much it says.

Appendix F Revert, Stopping and Selection Rules

Three rules decide which policy the loop carries and which one a run reports: the revert rule chooses the policy the next session edits, the stopping conditions end the run, and the selection rule picks the kept iterate. We give each rule and what it did in the runs, then relate the @kk of Table 1 to the kept iterate. Table 16 holds the thresholds and the per-task rates.

F.1 Revert Rule

The revert rule compares each training batch with the incumbent, the best iterate so far, lexicographically on per-object success rate, failed episodes that reached the goal geometry, median closest approach to the goal, and grasps that carried the object, each with a hysteresis margin (Table 16; 3 episodes, 20 mm, 3 carries); a lower key never overrules the direction of the success rate, and a batch in which every episode aborted is always a regression. On a regression the next session edits the incumbent instead of the latest iterate, and its report opens with a notice naming the undone edits (Listing E.3). We add the rule because in pilot runs sessions told that their last edit had regressed still built on it. The rule reads only training episodes. It fires after 18% of edited iterates (42% of these on success rate, 35% on closest approach, 21% on all-abort batches), most often where the margin is smallest relative to the batch: after 37% of Syringe Packing and 19% of Cable Routing edits (margins of 2/8 and 3/12 objects), against 5–15% on the one-object tasks.

F.2 Stopping Conditions

After each validation batch the harness checks, in order, the iteration cap, the validation target, the perfect-training streak (only in the runs without a validation set, Appendix C.2), the unchanged streak, the spend and the wall time, and stops at the first condition that holds (Table 16); a target met in the last iteration is recorded under the cap. The validation target replaces the first passes’ stop on two perfect training batches (Appendix F.4), since the agent edits against the training instances. The spend and wall time are runaway ceilings, not budgets; the unchanged streak and the spend never end a run. Most 6-iteration runs ran with a 30 h wall-time limit, and part of them with shorter episode budgets (1,400, 6,000, 2,400, 1,200–2,400 and 9,000 s in task order).

How the runs stop.

Of the 3-iteration runs, 54% stop at the cap and 46% on the target, 36% of all runs already at k=0k{=}0. Nearly every Gear Meshing and Cable Routing run meets its target (92% and 96%), mostly with π0\pi_{0}, and carries that reading forward, so these columns of Table 1 largely measure the zero-shot program. Syringe Packing never meets its target, so every Syringe run uses all its rounds. The 6-iteration runs, most without the expert skills, meet the target less often and later: 76% stop at the cap, 22% on the target (5% at k=0k{=}0) and 2% after two perfect training batches.

F.3 Kept Iterate

The kept iterate is the first iterate with the highest validation success, so an edit is kept only if it raises validation success. It is π0\pi_{0} in 70% of the 3-iteration runs, for three reasons that split by task (Table 16). Half of these runs meet the target with π0\pi_{0}, mostly on Gear Meshing and Cable Routing. A third never succeed on a validation instance, so every iterate ties at zero: on Tool Hanging no run of DeepSeek V4, Kimi K3 or either GPT-6 setting ever validates, nor any Kimi K3 run on USB-C Insertion, the repair failure of Finding 1 at its sharpest. In the remaining 15%, almost all on Syringe Packing, π0\pi_{0} validates at least as well as both edits. The 6-iteration runs keep π0\pi_{0} in 34% of runs, as they rarely stop at k=0k{=}0 and have five edits to improve on it. The runs without a validation set keep the revert rule’s incumbent, and one skill-library run, resumed to its iteration cap after a wall-time stop, keeps the iterate chosen at that stop.

F.4 Superseded First Passes

Three passes preceded the protocol of Appendix C. The first stopped after two perfect training batches and kept the iterate that trained best, and its first launch shipped the expert scripts with the reference library, so the agents copied the human solution; two of its runs enter the Opus 5, xhigh row of Table 1 (Appendix C.2), and its Tool Hanging run stopped with 70% held-out success. The second trained on four distinct instances but still stopped and selected on them; a brief third validated on three. Since the report describes exactly the training episodes, selecting on them rewards edits fitted to those layouts, so we moved stopping and selection to five validation instances the agent never sees and, in the feedback and skill-library studies, ship 𝒮τ\mathcal{S}_{\tau} only to the +𝒮τ+\,\mathcal{S}_{\tau} arm.

Appendix G Models and Inference

This appendix documents the ten agent settings of Table 1: models and access (Appendix G.1), call parameters (Appendix G.2), reasoning controls and realized thinking (Appendix G.3), and session statistics (Appendix G.4), the last two bearing on Finding 1. Appendix H gives the compute and cost of all three studies.

G.1 Models and Access

Table 17 identifies each setting by its model id, the date the id was first listed, and the dates its sessions ran. The Claude models run in the Claude Code CLI on a subscription login. Kimi K3 and DeepSeek V4 run in the same CLI against OpenRouter’s Anthropic-compatible endpoint, which keeps the prompt, tools, allowed commands and turn cap of the Claude settings and changes only the model. GPT-6 Astra and Sol run in OpenAI’s Codex CLI 0.155.1, which reads the same instruction file plus an AGENTS.md stating the workspace rules (Appendix D). The feedback and skill-library studies use the command and model of Opus 5, xhigh.

G.2 Inference Parameters

Table 18 gives the exact call of each CLI and every parameter the harness controls. We pass only what the CLIs expose: sampling stays at the provider defaults, every session has a 2-hour wall clock, and Claude Code caps sessions at 80 turns. From 2026-09-22, a rate-limited Claude session is rerun at once with the same model through OpenRouter, so a rate limit can change a session’s route but never its model or prompt.

G.3 Reasoning Budget

Controls and logged effort.

The harness sets a reasoning control only for Opus 5, high and low (thinking budgets of 32k and 4k tokens per request) and the two GPT-6 settings (Codex effort xhigh; Table 18). Claude Code’s effort level is left to each machine’s CLI settings. Where the logs record it, it is xhigh, except for 13% of the Opus 5, xhigh sessions (high, all on 2026-09-18) and most locally run Fable 5.1 sessions (medium); the remote machines record no level. Table 17 reports the sessions logged at xhigh per setting. In the feedback and skill-library studies these are the 26% of sessions run on the local machine; the rest ran on the remote machines.

Realized thinking.

The 32k and 4k budgets yield indistinguishable sessions (Table 17): median thinking of 17.8k and 18.6k tokens for initial programs and 21.2k and 15.4k for feedback rounds. The budget caps a single request, which rarely approaches it: Opus 5 thinks a median of 420 tokens per turn under the 32k budget and 387 under the 4k one. We therefore read the three Opus 5 rows as three samples of one model, not a sweep of reasoning effort (the xhigh row sets no budget and comes from 6-iteration runs, Appendix C.2). Read this way, they support Finding 1: the three rows start further apart (41–57%) than the six settings of DeepSeek V4, Sonnet 5, Kimi K3, Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 (33–45%), yet all three reach 74–81% at @2, far above the 44–48% at which DeepSeek V4, Sonnet 5, Kimi K3 and GPT-6 Astra end.

G.4 Agent Sessions

Table 19 summarizes the agent sessions. The median session lasts 3.0 to 11.8 minutes (DeepSeek V4: 29.0), far below the 2-hour limit, and takes 31–47 turns in Claude Code (Codex: 22 and 28 tool actions).

Turns and thinking do not track repair.

DeepSeek V4 takes the most turns, the longest sessions and the most thinking (69.2k tokens per feedback round), yet gains 6 points, while GPT-6 Sol gains 20 in 3-minute sessions that think 3.2k. Across the ten settings, the gain’s rank correlation with median turns (ρ=0.37\rho=0.37; 0.35 over the eight Claude Code settings alone), minutes (ρ=−0.22\rho=-0.22) and thinking per feedback round (ρ=0.09\rho=0.09) is weak; edit size tracks it (ρ=0.69\rho=0.69). The Opus 5 rows and Fable 5.1 change 113–196 lines per accepted edit and gain 17–40 points; Sonnet 5 and DeepSeek V4 change 27–30 lines and gain 1–6. Repair is thus not bought with more turns or thinking (Finding 1), and the models that repair little adjust their programs only slightly (Finding 2). Opus 5.5 edits little but starts highest (67% at @0). The exception is Sol, whose whole gain is USB-C Insertion (0% to 100%), reached with edits of 6–29 lines.

Fix sessions.

Most settings spend at most 14% of their sessions repairing a proposal the guard or validator rejected or a program that crashed in preflight (Appendix C.3). Kimi K3 (21%) and GPT-6 Sol (32%) spend the most; in both, the largest single source is one Gear Meshing run whose graph aborts before its first node runs. Kimi’s is repaired in its zero-shot round and scores 90%, Sol’s never passes the preflight and scores 0% in every round. Producing a program that loads is thus a hurdle separate from the behavioral repair that the gain measures.

Appendix H Compute and Cost

This appendix accounts for the study’s compute: the coding-agent sessions that write and edit the policies (Appendix H.1), the simulation that executes them (Appendix H.2), and the total LLM spend with the pilot and curriculum studies (Appendix H.3). Table 20 counts the runs, agent sessions, tokens, cost and simulation of every setting of Table 1 and of each study, with superseded passes and dropped arms in a row of their own. Neither Table 20 nor the study and pilot rows of Table 22 include the API calls that perception tools make inside the policies.

H.1 Agent Cost

Pricing.

Cost is repriced from each session’s tokens at the rates of Table 21, since Claude Code records Kimi K3 and DeepSeek V4 at Claude rates and the Codex CLI records no cost.

What drives cost.

Input tokens, mostly cache reads of the session’s growing context, outnumber output tokens more than twenty-fold in every setting, and cost follows the rates more than the token counts: Fable 5.1 reads the fewest input tokens of the Claude Code settings but costs the most, at twice Opus 5’s input, cache-write and output rates, while DeepSeek V4 writes the most output tokens but is the cheapest Claude Code setting, at under a tenth of Opus 5’s rates. Repairs of rejected proposals and crashing preflights add sessions but no feedback rounds; Kimi K3 and GPT-6 Sol spend 21% and 32% of their sessions on them (Table 19). Spend does not track success: Opus 5, high and Opus 5.5 each cost less than half as much as Fable 5.1 and end above it at @2 in Table 1 (81% and 77% against 64%).

H.2 Simulation

By task.

In each of the three studies, Syringe Packing and Cable Routing take most of the simulator time although they contribute fewer than half of the episodes: their episodes run the most control steps (their step caps are the two largest, Table 5), and Cable Routing is also the slowest task to simulate per step.

By split.

Across splits, the evaluation schedule (Table 11) decides where the time goes. A setting of Table 1 evaluates ten held-out instances every round, so held-out episodes take the largest share of its simulator time; the 6-iteration runs of the other two studies evaluate them only at k=0k{=}0 and on the kept iterate, so validation takes the largest share there.

H.3 Total LLM Spend

Table 22 totals the LLM spend of the paper: the four study rows of Table 20, the pilot study and the curriculum study. The pilot study covers the other Claude Code and Codex sessions on our development workstation, which also ran part of the study: those in its session logs, measured with ccusage, and older harness sessions, at the cost their transcripts record; older interactive sessions left no record, and the other study machines kept no logs of their sessions outside Table 20. The curriculum study’s spend is the figure its authors report. Nothing is counted twice: the study-run sessions of Table 20 are removed from the pilot study by session id, and the curriculum study ran on its authors’ machines.

Additional Results

 

Appendix I Failure Analysis

This appendix asks where the programs behind the paper’s tables fail. We define ten failure categories (Appendix I.1) and compare them across tasks (Appendix I.2) and across models and feedback rounds (Appendix I.3). A category marks where a failure becomes observable, possibly several skills after the decision that caused it (Finding 3). The harness’s own interventions (guard rejections, preflight crashes, reverts) are reported with the harness and its rules (Appendices C and F).

I.1 Taxonomy and Assignment

Unit.

The unit is the failed held-out object (two per Syringe Packing episode, three per Cable Routing episode, otherwise one; Table 5) of the zero-shot and @2 programs of every Table 1 run and of the kept programs of the feedback and restricted skill-library runs, scored with the final per-object rule of Appendix A.2. Pooled columns count each held-out batch once, so an initial program kept by several seeded arms counts once.

Precedence.

An episode’s failed objects take its category from the first rule that applies: (1) the outcome, step budget (U) or a diverged simulation or failed machine (I); (2) the message of the first node that raised, matched by keyword rules to P, G, K, T, B, or A for a placement check that raises; (3) a self-check abort (S) when the program routes itself to a failure end; (4) for a finished program the evaluator fails, A when the placement clause is unmet and R when only a rest, release or turning clause is. An error outranks the goal clause because a node that raises stops the program and leaves the placement unmet as a consequence. Of the final programs’ failed objects, 47% are assigned by the goal clause, 36% by an error message and 18% by the outcome or end node. Table 23 gives each rule with a verbatim example; the keyword rules were checked by eye on each category’s commonest messages. Held-out episodes store no trace, so a self-check abort cannot be traced to the check that fired.

I.2 Failures by Task

Table 24 gives the shares per task (left) and per study and reading (right). Placement is 49% of all failures and the largest category everywhere except Tool Hanging; 93% of it comes from programs that finish without an error while the object is misplaced.

Per task.

The categories beyond placement set the tasks apart.

  • •

    Tool Hanging fails mostly before the hook: 45% are planning refusals, three in five of them the planner rejecting every candidate grasp (plan_grasp: 0/1 candidate grasps had a feasible CuRobo plan …).

  • •

    Syringe Packing adds step budget (20%), perception (15%, mostly could not perceive 'medical syringe') and grasp failures (14%, mostly the program’s own in-hand check seeing no syringe follow the lifted hand) to placement (43%).

  • •

    Gear Meshing, which most programs solve, fails mostly with no gear seated (67%); most of its perception failures (17%) are programs that find no red start button (nothing red enough to be the button is visible).

  • •

    USB-C Insertion spreads over placement (36%, nearly all a plug short of the insertion depth), planning refusals (18%, e.g. no reachable transit above the plug) and grasp misses (17%); its program bugs (5%) all come from the seeded arms’ inherited initial policy, which calls usbc.receptacle_shape on a port the tool does not describe.

  • •

    Cable Routing adds self-check aborts (20%, more than half to an end node named unfinished) to placement (69%).

I.3 Failures by Model and Feedback Round

Figure 16 splits the @0 and @2 columns of Table 24 by model.

Pooled.

From @0 to @2, perception (11→\rightarrow7%), grasp (13→\rightarrow11%), reach (9→\rightarrow5%) and program-bug failures (3→\rightarrow0%) shrink while placement (31→\rightarrow39%) and step budget (8→\rightarrow14%) grow: improved programs fail later in the task. The program bugs that still reach held-out episodes escape the single preflight episode, and none survives to @2. Both growing categories mostly carry no error message, so their cause must be traced back from intermediate outcomes, the attribution problem of Finding 3.

By model.

Planning refusals, flat at 16% pooled, separate the models. The three Opus 5 rows, Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 cut them to at most 6% at @2, leaving placement as their largest category (43–60%); on Tool Hanging, Opus 5, low, Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 move from failing mainly at the planner to failing mainly at the hook. GPT-6 Astra cuts them as well (to 6%) but trades them for grasp failures (13→\rightarrow32%). DeepSeek V4, Sonnet 5, Kimi K3 and GPT-6 Sol have 16–35% at @2; on Tool Hanging, which they leave at 0–2%, planning refusals are each model’s largest category. For DeepSeek V4, feedback repaired the perception behind 70% of its @0 Tool Hanging failures only to expose planning refusals behind all of its @2 ones. Models that start alike thus stall at different stages (Finding 1), and four of the five models that stall on Tool Hanging stall where a collision-aware planner refuses their grasp or path (Finding 5); GPT-6 Astra stalls at the hook (85% of its @2 Tool Hanging failures are placement).

Standard Deviation
Other studies.

The feedback study’s kept programs fail at placement more often (63%) than Table 1’s @2 programs (39%) and never at the grasp. The restricted skill-library arms’ perception share (25%) comes entirely from the tools-only arm on Cable Routing, which segments no cable in any held-out episode.

Curriculum Study

 

Appendix J Privileged-to-Perception Curriculum

This appendix provides the full experimental details for the curriculum study in Section 5.4 (Figure 10 and Table 4). Section J.1 describes the two learning settings, tool access, tasks, training and evaluation protocol, and the conversion from privileged geometry to perception. Section J.2 then analyzes representative cases in which transfer is unsuccessful.

J.1 Experimental Setup

J.1.1 Settings and Agent

Learning settings.

We compare two settings that use the same self-learning loop (Section 3), model, instructions, skill library, feedback, training layouts, and total iteration budget. They differ only in how the policy observes the scene.

  • •

    Privileged →\rightarrow perception (w/ curr.). For the first KpK_{p} iterations, the policy observes exact simulator geometry and has no camera access. We then convert the best privileged checkpoint to a perception policy and continue learning for KvK_{v} iterations using perception only.

  • •

    Perception only (w/o curr.). The policy uses cameras and perception tools for all Kp+KvK_{p}+K_{v} iterations.

MimicGen and VABAR runs use different configurations, described in Section J.1.4. Within each suite, the privileged →\rightarrow perception and perception-only settings use the same model, probe allowance, feedback format, training and held-out layouts, iteration budget, and evaluation protocol; they differ only in the scene information available to the policy.

On MimicGen, we use Claude Fable 5.1 with Kp=Kv=8K_{p}=K_{v}=8 (16 iterations per run). On VABAR, we use Claude Opus 5 with Kp=Kv=5K_{p}=K_{v}=5 (10 iterations per run). We run each setting three times per task (runs 000, 001, and 002), giving 7×3=217\times 3=21 curriculum runs and 21 perception-only runs.

Initial policies.

Iteration 0 is a zero-shot policy written by the agent from the task instruction and skill library. In the perception-only setting, each run starts from a fixed zero-shot perception policy shared with the other perception-only studies in the paper. In the privileged setting, the agent writes a separate zero-shot policy using the privileged tool surface, because a perception policy cannot execute with the privileged tool list. On VABAR, run 000 in each setting uses the first workflow graph produced for that run, while runs 001 and 002 are generated in new sessions from the same frozen prompt and model without additional training.

Agent harness.

The agent is Claude Code with temperature 0.2. It can read, write, and search files in the policy workspace, run ./validate.sh, and copy library skills into the workspace. It cannot invoke the simulator directly, except on MimicGen, where it may call ./probe.sh for probe episodes (Appendix J.1.5). Each improvement step starts a new session that receives the current policy, the latest feedback report, and a summary of previous iterations and code changes. On MimicGen, a session is limited to 35 turns, 10 minutes of active time, and 45 minutes total. On VABAR, a session is limited to 80 turns with no wall-clock limit, as in the other VABAR experiments. The conversion session uses the same turn limit and no wall-clock limit.

J.1.2 Tool Access

Privileged tools.

During the privileged phase, the policy observes the scene only through simulator geometry queries: sim.list_objects, sim.get_object_pose, and sim.get_object_obb provide exact object poses and oriented bounding boxes, while sim.list_features and sim.get_feature provide world-frame geometry for named functional parts. These parts are defined by the task assets; examples include the needle handle and shaft in Threading, the stove burner in Kitchen, the machine holder and lid in Coffee, the drawer handle and floor in Mug Cleanup, and each wrench ring and hook shank in Tool Hanging. VABAR additionally provides sim.list_regions and sim.get_region_obb for regions, and sim.get_fixture_layout for multi-part fixtures without a single object pose, such as the peg centers, pinion center, and button on the Gear Meshing board.

All camera and perception tools are disabled during this phase, including RGB-D observations, Grounding DINO detection, SAM3 segmentation and tracking, and geometry helpers that recover 3D structure from masks and depth. Robot control, motion, and grasp skills are unchanged. The agent is explicitly instructed to learn task decomposition and manipulation logic that can later be executed from RGB-D observations, and not to hard-code poses observed in feedback.

Perception tools.

The perception policy observes the scene only through calibrated cameras that provide RGB, depth, intrinsics, and camera pose. MimicGen uses the fixed agentview camera and a wrist camera; VABAR uses each task’s own camera set: fixed overhead, front, side, or top-down views, plus wrist cameras in Tool Hanging and USB-C Insertion. The policy can use Grounding DINO for text-prompted bounding boxes, SAM3 for masks from text, boxes, or points, and geometry utilities that back-project masks and depth into world coordinates and fit boxes, lines, and planes. All sim.* geometry queries are disabled.

In both settings, the policy never receives task flags, goal predicates, success checks, or task-specific planners. These signals are used only for scoring and feedback.

Tool enforcement.

Each setting uses a fixed tool list. Before an edited policy can run, a validator checks every policy script and rejects any call outside the allowed tool surface, including calls constructed dynamically at run time. The agent must pass this check with ./validate.sh before the session ends. If the check fails, the violation is returned to the agent for up to two repair rounds.

J.1.3 Tasks

Table 26 lists the seven tasks used in the study. We select tasks that require both accurate state estimation and non-trivial manipulation, so that separating perception from manipulation can meaningfully affect learning.

  • •

    Threading and Coffee require precise insertion. A failure can therefore arise from target localization, the object’s pose in the gripper, or the insertion motion itself.

  • •

    Kitchen and Mug Cleanup are long, multi-stage tasks with articulated objects, so errors early in the trajectory can affect later stages.

  • •

    Tool Hanging (Level 2) contains two wrenches, two hooks, and distractor tools. Each wrench must be grasped so that its ring remains available for hanging and the object remains stable during transport.

  • •

    Gear Meshing (Level 2) requires placing three gears on thin pegs so that they mesh with a fixed pinion, followed by a button press.

  • •

    USB-C Insertion (Level 1) requires aligning a small plug with a receptacle to within a few millimeters and inserting it to sufficient depth.

In the privileged phase, task-relevant parts such as rings, pegs, and ports are available through exact geometry, which largely removes localization error. After conversion, the same structures must be recovered from RGB-D observations, including small or low-contrast parts.

J.1.4 Differences Between MimicGen and VABAR Runs

For each benchmark, the two curriculum settings use the same experimental configuration. The VABAR experiments use the same setup as the other VABAR experiments in this paper: Claude Opus 5, text-only feedback, a fixed set of four training layouts, no probe episodes, and sessions of up to 80 turns with no time limit.

For MimicGen, we adapt this setup to make self-learning more tractable because its tasks present a harder learning problem. MimicGen tasks are long-horizon, multi-stage, and involve multiple objects. For example, Kitchen requires the agent to interact with the stove, pot, bread, and serving area in the correct sequence over a 1500-step episode. Moreover, the skill library contains no task-specific skills for most MimicGen tasks, so the agent must develop the task-specific skills needed to solve them during self-learning. Object configurations are also randomized over a wide range, making it easy for a policy trained on a fixed set of layouts to overfit.

We therefore use a stronger model for MimicGen (Claude Fable 5.1), provide failure-image feedback, allow more learning iterations and training episodes, resample training seeds at every iteration to reduce overfitting, and include probe episodes so that the agent can test a hypothesis before modifying its policy. Because MimicGen learning runs are longer (16 iterations), we additionally limit each session to 35 turns and 10 minutes of agent update time. This encourages each iteration to make a more localized policy update. The differences between the VABAR and MimicGen configurations are summarized in Table 27.

J.1.5 Training and Evaluation

Training, held-out, and probe layouts.

On MimicGen, each iteration trains on 10 newly sampled layouts, with training layouts not reused across iterations. The agent may additionally run up to two unscored probe episodes per iteration to test a hypothesis. Because VABAR contains fewer layouts, each iteration instead uses the same four fixed training layouts, one episode per layout, and probe episodes are disabled. In both cases, the agent is told that evaluation uses unseen layouts and that movable objects must therefore be localized at run time.

After every iteration, the policy is evaluated on 10 fixed held-out layouts that are disjoint from training. Held-out results are never shown to the agent; they are used only to construct the learning curves and to select the privileged checkpoint for conversion. Within each benchmark, the curriculum and perception-only settings use the same training sequence and the same held-out layouts.

One learning iteration.

Each iteration has three stages. (1) Preflight: the current policy runs on two unscored episodes of at most 300 steps to detect program errors. If it crashes, the agent receives the error and may perform up to two repair sessions. (2) Training: the policy runs on the training layouts and a feedback report is generated. (3) Improvement: a new agent session reads the report and edits the policy; the resulting policy must pass the tool validator. Held-out evaluation of the new policy runs in parallel with the next learning iteration. We do not revert edits or stop runs early, so every run uses its full iteration budget.

Feedback.

Both settings receive the same feedback structure. The report describes object states and inter-object relations using named object parts and object-centered frames, organized by the named steps of the policy (Section 3). For each episode, it also reports which ordered reference stages were reached (Table 26) and the corresponding stage reward: the number of stages completed in order before the first missed stage, divided by the total number of stages and averaged across episodes. Up to two episodes are shown in full detail, and the previous six iterations are summarized as history. MimicGen reports additionally include two end-of-episode agentview frames to provide richer feedback and further facilitate learning, whereas VABAR reports are text only. The privileged and perception-only settings therefore differ in policy observations, not in the feedback used for self-improvement.

Metrics.

We report held-out success after every iteration: native task success on MimicGen and per-object success on VABAR (for example, each wrench or gear is scored separately). We also report held-out stage reward. In Figure 10, each line is the mean across the three runs and the shaded band shows ±1\pm 1 standard error. In Table 4, # Skills is the number of nodes in the final policy workflow graph, where each node is one code-executing step, and Success is the mean held-out success over the last three iterations; both are averaged across the three runs.

J.1.6 Conversion to Perception

At the end of the privileged phase, we select the privileged checkpoint with the highest held-out success, breaking ties by stage reward and then by the latest iteration. A dedicated conversion session receives the selected policy, its most recent feedback report, and the perception tool list, together with the following instruction:

The privileged perception phase is over. This checkpoint must now run on the vision-only tool surface. Preserve its task decomposition, manipulation logic, recovery branches, and bounded diagnostics. Replace every privileged sim geometry read and every privileged perception skill with calibrated RGB-D perception using the shipped vision skills and tools. Do not hard-code object poses observed in the privileged phase. Finish only when ./validate.sh reports OK on the vision surface.

The conversion session uses the same turn limit as a normal improvement session and has no wall-clock limit. It does not execute the policy or receive new environment feedback, so the first perception iteration evaluates the converted policy exactly as produced by the conversion session. All 21 conversions passed the validator on the first attempt, with conversion costs of 12–39 minutes and $5–15 in API usage. The converted checkpoint then becomes the starting policy for the perception phase.

J.2 Failure Analysis of Unsuccessful Transfer

We further analyze the failure modes observed in the curriculum study from Section 5.4. Figure 17 illustrates representative examples and reveals two distinct limitations of privileged-to-perception learning. First, policies learned with exact geometry may rely on a level of geometric precision that perception cannot reliably recover after transfer. Second, exact geometry alone may be insufficient for learning the object affordances and contact strategies required for robust manipulation.

Dependence on privileged geometric precision.

Policies learned with exact geometry can inherit manipulation strategies that are highly sensitive to localization errors after transfer to perception, as illustrated in Figure 17(a). In Kitchen, the privileged policy in one run achieves 90–100% held-out success by pinching a narrow tab on the pot handle using exact geometry. After transfer to perception, success drops to 0–30% and eventually reaches 0%. The agent repeatedly identifies the tab grasp as the source of failure, but modifies its reaching and retry behavior rather than adopting a more robust grasp. Because the usable grasp region is only a few millimeters wide, the inherited strategy is highly sensitive to perceptual error.

Gear Meshing shows a related failure in one run. Held-out success drops from 70–90% before transfer to at most 7% afterward. The inherited policy can still grasp and carry the gears, but after transfer it must recover the peg locations from vision. The policy uses the front camera, where each peg occupies only 2–3 raised depth pixels, rather than the overhead camera, where each occupies about 18 pixels (Figure 17(a)). As a result, the short pegs are often merged with the plate or missed entirely, leaving the policy without a valid placement target. In contrast, a perception-only run that uses the overhead camera reaches 97–100% held-out success. Subsequent iterations mainly try to repair peg detection, rather than changing the inherited camera choice or manipulation strategy. Together with Kitchen, this shows that privileged learning can produce effective strategies that become brittle when they depend on geometric precision that perception cannot reliably recover.

Manipulation failures despite exact geometry.

Exact geometry alone may also be insufficient for understanding object affordances and selecting robust manipulation strategies, as illustrated in Figure 17(b). In Tool Hanging, the privileged state provides the exact wrench pose but does not specify where or how the wrench should be grasped for reliable transport. Consequently, the agent learns to grasp the wrench near its far end, resulting in an unstable grasp during the subsequent carry motion. Because the resulting failure becomes apparent only during transport, the agent struggles to attribute it to the earlier grasp decision and fails to learn an effective strategy. Privileged training never exceeds 10% held-out success in any of the three runs, whereas perception-only learning reaches 60–100%.

USB-C Insertion reveals a related limitation in contact reasoning. In one privileged training run, the policy consistently aligns the plug with the bore but fails during insertion because contact with the socket causes the plug to tilt and become wedged. The controller fails to recover from this contact-induced error, resulting in 0% success. These examples show that exact geometry can reduce localization error without providing the affordance understanding and contact reasoning needed for robust manipulation.
